title: Fats & Oils
subtitle: 300 BC–600 AD · Oil Empire and Butter Frontier: Rome’s Oil Jars, the Tripolitanian Boom, Ghee and Sesame in India and the First Pressed Oils of China

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Egypt’s five taxed oils, Caesar’s fine on Leptis and the oil annona

entries.label: Ptolemy II taxes five oils, castor among them
entries.hint: Under Ptolemy II the Revenue Laws taxed five oils: Dalby notes castor oil among them, an oil used in lamps but seldom for food. Egypt’s oil came from plants such as castor, sesame and safflower, not from the olive, which Pharaonic Egypt had imported from Palestine.
entries.note: SECONDARY (papyrus not read): Dalby, Food in the Ancient World from A to Z (2003), ‘castor oil’ (‘one of the five oils taxed under Ptolemy II’; ‘used for lamps but seldom for food’) and the Egypt entry citing Grenfell’s edition of the Revenue Laws of Ptolemy Philadelphus; ‘Pharaonic Egypt imported olive oil from Palestine’ is from the ‘olive oil’ entry. The date 259 BC is the conventional date of the papyrus, not given in the extracted text; Dalby’s text is multi-column and partly garbled.

entries.label: Caesar fines Leptis three million pounds of oil
entries.hint: After the civil war the town of Leptis was fined 3 million Roman pounds of olive oil for backing the wrong side. Mattingly argues the town was Lepcis Magna, and that if the fine was annual it would be only 10–25 per cent of average production, so a total of 4–10 million litres a year; three million pounds is about 980,000 kg or 1.07 million litres.
entries.note: CONTESTED (annual or one-off; which Leptis): Mattingly, ‘The Olive Boom’, Libyan Studies 19 (1988) pp.21–48 (appendix), citing Bellum Africum 97.3; the production figures are his hypothetical order-of-magnitude estimates. The year 46 BC is the date of the African war, not stated in the passage read.

entries.label: Lepcis’s oil gift to Rome and the oil annona of Tripolitania
entries.hint: After Septimius Severus granted Lepcis the Ius Italicum, the city voluntarily gave Rome a gift of oil; this donation probably prompted a new post, an official ‘procurator ad olea conparanda per regionem Tripolitanam’ for the oil annona, first attested perhaps under Severus Alexander. Mattingly counts it, with the absorption of land into imperial estates, as a step that took much of the region’s surplus out of local control.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly argument): Mattingly, Tripolitania (2003 ed.) pp.92–93 (the oil donation and the procurator) and p.123 (stamped oil amphorae of the early 3rd century and the Ius Italicum); Mattingly (1988) abstract (the voluntary ‘tax’ in olive oil). The motive is Mattingly’s inference, and the post’s first attestation is not precisely dated.

entries.label: The Buddha’s five medicines: ghee, butter, oil, honey and syrup
entries.hint: In the Pali Vinaya’s chapter on medicine sick monks may take five tonics even after midday: ghee, butter, oil, honey and syrup (molasses). Two of the five are fats and one is a sweetener, so the earliest Buddhist rule for the sick monk is a list of fats and sugars.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Pali not read): the same Vinaya passage is sourced in sugar-300bc-600ad::b1 (Mahāvagga VI, Pācittiya 39, as summarised on SuttaCentral-derived pages; Needham SCC 6.3 p.68 on the five medicines). The Vinaya’s redaction is placed 4th–1st century BC, so the date is a span. Compare the Pātimokkha syrup in sugar-1200bc-300bc::b3.

entries.label: Sidonius Apollinaris: a Burgundian ‘perfumed with rancid butter’
entries.hint: The Gallo-Roman bishop and poet Sidonius Apollinaris complains of living among the occupying Germans, applauding despite himself the song of a drunken Burgundian ‘his head perfumed with rancid butter’. Butter is the fat of the barbarian north, used even as hair dressing, at the point where the Mediterranean’s oil world meets the north’s butter world.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; the poem not read): Khosrova, Butter (2016) ch.3 (PDF p.55), who calls him ‘a fourth-century Roman bishop and poet’; Sidonius wrote in the 460s–470s, so the folio dates it to the 470s, an inference from his career, not from Khosrova.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Galen and Anthimus on butter; Caraka on ghee and sesame; the Chinese farm manual

entries.label: Caraka and Suśruta: ghee in autumn, sesame oil for frying, sixty oilseeds
entries.hint: Indian medical texts of the early centuries AD already show a move from ghee to oil: Caraka advises ghee only in the autumn, animal body fats in spring and vegetable oils in the rains, and prizes sesame oil as a base for medicines and for frying; Suśruta counts sixty oilseeds and urges moderation in kitchen oil. Achaya says the old Aryan preference for ghee as a cooking medium had softened by the early Christian era.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Sanskrit not read): Achaya, Indian Food Tradition (1994) p.83 (PDF p.101, OCR of a scanned PDF) — Caraka’s seasonal rule, sesame oil, sixty oilseeds in Suśruta, animal fats (tallow, lard, marrow). The Caraka and Suśruta datings follow the Sugar folio (sugar-300bc-600ad::th9: 1st–2nd and c.4th centuries).

entries.label: Galen: butter for the barbarians’ bath and for poultices
entries.hint: The physician Galen says that in cold regions that lack olive oil people use butter for washing themselves, and that Greek and Roman medicine uses butter in poultices and other medicaments as it uses hard fats. Butter has a place in the medicine chest but not on the Greek or Roman table.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; Galen not read): Khosrova (2016) ch.3 (PDF pp.54–55) quoting Galen (‘People in many cold regions where they lack olive oil use butter for washing themselves’; ‘We also use it as we use hard fats, mixing it onto poultices’). The date is Galen’s career, as in the Sugar folios.

entries.label: Anthimus: fresh unsalted butter for consumption
entries.hint: The Byzantine physician Anthimus, in On the Observance of Foods, prescribes fresh butter, without salt, with a little honey, to be licked at intervals while lying down, for ‘consumption’ (tuberculosis).
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history): Khosrova (2016) ch.3 (PDF p.55) quoting Anthimus, ‘a Byzantine physician’ of the sixth century; the dating to the 510s–530s is the folio’s inference from Anthimus’s career and was not checked.

entries.label: The Chhi min yao shu: colza oil mills and the fats of the kitchen
entries.hint: The agricultural manual Chhi min yao shu (finished 544) shows pressing colza for oil as an established commercial activity: 200 piculs of seed from 100 mou sold to the oil mills, worth as much as 600 piculs of hulled grain. It records perilla, sesame and hemp oils in cooking, lighting and oiling cloth, rating sesame oil best for frying; yet the recipes still prefer lard and tallow for roasting and frying.
entries.note: SECONDARY (translation read in Needham): Needham, Science and Civilisation in China 6.5 (2000) pp.439–440 (PDF pp.467–468), Table 41 and notes 14–20 (CMYS ch.18 p.133, ch.26 p.154, ch.78 p.485, ch.80 p.494). Needham’s own statement is that vegetable oils were ‘a significant component of the economy’ by the 6th century while ‘animal grease remained the preferred fatty ingredient’.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Monte Testaccio, the Tripolitanian boom, hemp oil, the Arthaśāstra

entries.label: Monte Testaccio: fifty million oil jars
entries.hint: Monte Testaccio in Rome is a man-made hill of over 50 million amphorae, mostly olive-oil containers, thrown away after their contents were emptied into the city’s great oil warehouses; most of the stamps and painted labels come from the globular Dressel 20 jars of southern Spain. On Rodríguez Almeida’s reading Rome imported of the order of 10 million litres of oil a year, a figure Mattingly thinks may be conservative.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Mattingly, Tripolitania (2003 ed.) ch.on the amphorae (‘over 50 million amphorae’, Dressel’s study of CIL XV) and ‘The Olive Boom’ (1988), Rodríguez Almeida 1984 for the 10 million litres. The dump built up over the 100s–200s AD on the general chronology of the hill; the passage read does not give dates, so the span is the folio’s from common knowledge and should be checked against Blázquez (not in the library).

entries.label: The Tripolitanian olive boom
entries.hint: In Roman Tripolitania the territory of Lepcis contained many hundreds of olive presses, perhaps as many as 1,500, with a potential output of millions of litres in a good year; a few press complexes were ‘oileries’. Mattingly argues that this oil surplus made the Lepcitanian elite so rich that its sons entered the Senate, and in AD 193 produced the first African emperor, Septimius Severus. After Severus’s sons were killed by 217 the town’s fortunes declined.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly argument; archaeology from surveys): Mattingly, Tripolitania (2003 ed.) ch.on economy and trade (‘many hundreds of olive presses (perhaps as many as 1,500)’; Oates’s Fergian survey: 63 sites with 126 presses; the Sofeggin and Zem-Zem presses, over 60) and ‘The Olive Boom’ (1988) abstract. Mattingly himself calls the quantification ‘a series of hypotheses’.

entries.label: Twenty litres a head: how much oil the Roman world used
entries.hint: Using a rule of thumb of about 20 litres of oil a head a year in the oil-rich heartlands, Mattingly reckons that a Mediterranean population of 25–50 million would have needed 500 million to 1,000 million litres a year. He argues the oil’s importance — as food, as the main lighting fuel and as the base of medicines, soaps and perfumes — has been seriously underestimated.
entries.note: CONTESTED (an estimate on an estimate): Mattingly (1988) introduction, citing Amouretti 1986 pp.177–196 and Forbes & Foxhall 1978; Foxhall, Olive Cultivation in Ancient Greece (2007) ch.4, Table 4.1 estimates 25–35 kg a person a year for food alone in a wealthy Athenian household. Both are modern calculations, not ancient records.

entries.label: Ten thousand piculs of hemp oil in one warehouse
entries.hint: The Record of the Investigation of Things (c.290) mentions heating hemp-seed oil to drive off water and the fire hazard of ten thousand piculs of oil accumulated in a single warehouse — an early record of oil stored as a trade commodity.
entries.note: SECONDARY (translation read in Needham): Needham, SCC 6.5 (2000) p.437 (PDF p.465), citing Po wu chi ch.3 p.6a; the author states that the actual pressing of seeds ‘was not accomplished until the late Han’ and that the word yu is not seen in antiquity. The Po wu chi is Needham’s ‘next occurrence of the word yu in the sense of an oil’ after the Han references.

entries.label: Oil in the Arthaśāstra meat shop
entries.hint: The Arthaśāstra of Kauṭilya, which Achaya dates to about AD 300, gives the proportions for dressing 20 palas (about 700 g) of fresh meat in a shop: one kuduba (250 g) of oil, two-thirds of a kuduba of curds, one pala of salt and a fifth of a pala of pungent spices — an early record of oil as a commercial cooking medium and of state supervision of slaughter.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Sanskrit not read): Achaya (1994) p.55 (PDF p.73). Date follows Achaya (‘about AD 300’); the Sugar folio treats the Arthaśāstra as a text with layers from about 100 BC (sugar-300bc-600ad::te1), so the date is a dispute.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Roman presses, China’s first pressing, soap as drug

entries.label: The Roman beam press, the screw press and the olive mill
entries.hint: Cato’s farming manual gives the first written description of a beam press for olives. Pliny lists the beam press, two lever types and the screw press; Hero describes two lever and two screw presses; a wedge press is painted in the House of the Vettii at Pompeii; and Pliny describes the roller mill (mola olearia) for crushing olives. In mechanical presses for oil the West was far ahead of China.
entries.note: SECONDARY (survey read): Needham, SCC 6.5 (2000) pp.437–439 (PDF pp.465–467) with Figs 94–95, summarising Forbes (1956), Cato De agri cultura x–xiii, Pliny NH, Hero Mechanica III and Drachmann (1932); Needham dates Cato ‘−3rd century’ (Cato wrote c.160 BC). Compare the Greek beam press in fats-1200bc-300bc::te1.

entries.label: China learns to press oil from seeds
entries.hint: Before the Han there is no record of pressing any seed for oil in China; the cooking fats of the Zhou li and Li ji are animal fats. Needham concludes that pressing was not accomplished until the late Han, nearly two thousand years after the olive press in the Mediterranean; by the Chhi min yao shu of 544 colza pressing was a commercial activity.
entries.note: CONTESTED (argument from silence): Needham, SCC 6.5 (2000) pp.28–29 (PDF p.56) and p.437 (PDF p.465) — ‘the actual pressing of the seeds … was not accomplished until the late Han’. It rests on the absence of records, so a date for the first pressing is not established. See fats-1200bc-300bc::th2 for the Zhou fats.

entries.label: Soap is known, as a cosmetic and a medicine
entries.hint: Soap was known in antiquity, but its early uses were cosmetic and medicinal, and when its cleansing power came to be widely recognised is not clear. For Greeks and Romans the working cleanser was still olive oil rubbed on and scraped off, and olive oil itself was a soap, a cosmetic, and the fuel of lamps.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Ward, The Clean Body: A Modern History (2019) ch.on soap, section ‘The art of soap making’ (‘while soap was known in antiquity, its early uses were cosmetic and medicinal’); Dalby (2003), ‘olive oil’ (‘It was a fuel, especially for lamps. It was a soap, or cosmetic’). The date is a placeholder for the Roman imperial period.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Tripolitanian oil to Rome; sesame to China; ghee and oil from India

entries.label: Sesame reaches China by the Silk Road
entries.hint: Chinese tradition says sesame was brought from the west by the general Zhang Qian in the 100s BC, probably along the Silk Road; the Chinese name hu ma (‘foreign hemp’) marks its overseas introduction. By the 500s it was the best cooking oil in the Chhi min yao shu, though not yet recorded as being pressed.
entries.note: SECONDARY (later tradition): Bedigian (ed.), Sesame: The Genus Sesamum (2011) ch.1 p.6 (PDF p.31), citing the Pen ts’ao kang mu (1596) for the Zhang Qian tradition (the introduction is dated by that late source, so treat it as a tradition); Needham SCC 6.5 p.439 on sesame oil as the best frying oil. See also sugar-1200bc-300bc::th1 for the traffic of words.

entries.label: The Periplus: ghee and sesame oil among India’s exports
entries.loc: Barygaza and south India, to Africa and Rome
entries.hint: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea lists ghee and sesame oil among the goods carried from Indian ports to the market towns of the African coast, and Achaya adds that it records coconut oil exported from the south in the 1st century AD, and that ghee was sent in leather skins from south India to Rome.
entries.note: SECONDARY: the Periplus §14 list (wheat, rice, ghee, sesame oil, cotton cloth) is sourced in sugar-300bc-600ad::x1; Achaya, Indian Food Tradition (1994) p.47 (PDF p.65, OCR) for the coconut-oil export and the ghee ‘called butyron’ sent to Rome (without a reference in the passage read). The Periplus text itself was not read here.

entries.label: Tripolitanian oil in Rome and the Mediterranean
entries.hint: Tripolitanian oil reached Rome and Ostia in its own amphorae, whose stamps show elite estates controlling the trade; on some Ostian evidence its share of Rome’s oil imports averaged nearer 10 per cent. Even a 1–5 per cent share of the city’s imports would be an export above a million litres a year — the same size as Caesar’s fine.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly argument): Mattingly (1988) section on trade and appendix (Panella 1977, 1983 for the Ostia evidence; the stamps and the Ius Italicum link in Tripolitania (2003 ed.) p.123). Shipwreck evidence is slight, as Mattingly notes.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Germanic revenge of animal fat

entries.label: The Germanic peoples bring the revenge of animal fat on imperial oil
entries.hint: When the Germanic peoples overran the western Empire in the 400s and 500s, Mueller argues, they brought a cuisine of meat, beer and animal fat in place of the Greco-Roman bread, wine and olive oil. Pork entered the Roman annona beside oil; forests came to be measured in hogs; calendar scenes of the olive harvest gave way to pigs on acorns; and Anthimus, physician at Theodoric’s court, praised the lard the northerners used as dressing and even ate raw as a cure-all.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; one author’s interpretation): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the section opening ‘Cookbooks, like histories, are written by the victors’ (the revenge of ‘animal fat on imperial oil’; pork in the annona; the calendars; Anthimus on lard). I have not found the other studies Mueller draws on. Compare th2: Khosrova quotes Anthimus on butter, Mueller on lard.
